analysis.one_liner: Reinstates the ban on exporting U.S. crude oil and natural gas, and lets the President restrict coal exports too.
analysis.headline: The bill to reinstate the crude oil export ban had three Democratic Senate sponsors, was sent to the Banking Committee, and never got a hearing or vote before the 116th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would undo the 2015 decision to allow U.S. crude oil exports. It requires the President to write a rule banning exports of American crude oil and natural gas, with exemptions the President can grant for reasons of national interest. It also gives the President authority to restrict exports of coal, refined petroleum products, petrochemical feedstocks, and even energy equipment, while protecting routine trade with Canada and Mexico. Supporters' goal was to keep American energy at home so domestic consumers face lower fuel prices; producers would lose the ability to sell to foreign buyers.
analysis.who_benefits: If the bill had passed, American households and businesses could have benefited from somewhat lower gasoline, heating fuel, and natural gas prices, since more domestic supply would stay in the U.S. market. Climate-focused groups also favored keeping fossil fuels in the ground or at home. It protects normal cross-border energy trade with Canada and Mexico.

how_it_helps.text: Requires the President to issue a rule prohibiting exports of crude oil and natural gas produced in the United States, reversing the 2015 repeal of the export ban.
Repeals the legalization of crude oil exports enacted in the Consolidated Appropriations Act of 2016 by striking its key subsections.
Allows exemptions from the ban where the President determines exports serve the national interest, including by purpose, buyer, or destination country.
Preserves uninterrupted energy trade with Canada and Mexico, recognizing historical trading relations with the two neighbors.

analysis.who_pays: Oil and gas producers would lose access to foreign buyers and the world prices they can command, likely reducing domestic drilling revenue and jobs in producing regions. Coal producers and exporters would face possible new export restrictions. Trading partners could retaliate against other U.S. exports.

drawbacks.text: Blocking exports pushes more domestic oil and gas onto the U.S. market, which can depress prices enough to reduce domestic production, cutting royalties, tax revenue, and jobs in energy-producing states.

The bill's export restrictions are broad: they cover coal, refined products, petrochemical feedstocks, and energy equipment, not just crude oil, which could disrupt export-dependent industries well beyond the oil patch.
Economists generally note that export bans can invite retaliation from trading partners and can raise world prices by removing supply, offsetting some of the benefit to U.S. consumers.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill aimed at a real consumer benefit—keeping domestically produced fuel home to hold down prices—but the evidence that an export ban delivers large savings is limited, and the costs to producers and export jobs in oil, gas, and coal regions would be immediate and concentrated. The very broad scope (covering coal, refined products, and even equipment) made it a sweeping restriction rather than a narrow consumer measure. It never advanced far enough for anyone to test these trade-offs in practice.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the Senate Banking Committee the day it was introduced and never received a hearing, markup, or vote; it died there when the 116th Congress ended in January 2021.

narrative.text: Sen. Edward Markey introduced the BAN Oil Exports Act on September 19, 2019, for himself and Sens. Merkley and Wyden.
The Senate read the bill twice and referred it to the Committee on Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs the same day.
The bill's only two cosponsors were Democrats, and no further action of any kind was taken on it.
The 116th Congress ended on January 3, 2021, with the bill still sitting in committee.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Oil and gas producers kept their export markets and world prices, and the coal industry avoided new export restrictions. Consumers never got the chance to see whether keeping fuel at home would have lowered their prices.

for.name: Edward Markey
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to reinstate the crude oil export ban.

against.name: Senate Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs Committee
against.role: Committee of referral, chaired by a Republican
against.what_they_did: Took no action on the bill after referral — no hearing, no markup, no vote.

against.name: Mike Crapo
against.role: Chair, Senate Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs Committee
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled committee action on the bill, leaving it to die at the end of the Congress.

against.name: Oil and gas producers
against.what_they_did: Opposed reinstating the crude export ban, which would have cut off their foreign customers.

sides.party_line_note: All three sponsors were Democrats and no Republican cosponsored; the Senate, run by Republicans, never brought the bill to any vote.

industries.note: The bill would ban exports of U.S. crude oil and natural gas, cutting producers off from foreign buyers and world prices. Their export revenue comes at the cost of higher domestic fuel prices, so their interest runs against household energy costs in this fight.
The President could restrict coal exports under the bill, threatening revenue for an export-dependent industry. Restrictions would aim at keeping fuel supplies domestic.

Keeping crude, refined products, and petrochemical feedstocks at home would lower feedstock costs for domestic refiners and chemical manufacturers. Their gain would come from the same cheap-domestic-supply effect consumers would benefit from.
